1.pericope_label: And I saw when the Lamb opened one of the seals, and I heard, as it were the noise of thunder, one of the four beasts saying, Come and see

schools.summary: Say plainly where the difficulty begins. This chapter contains the opening of six of the seven seals, and it is here that interpreters begin to differ, and here that commences the divergence toward those various, discordant, and many of them wild and fantastic theories which have been proposed in the exposition of this book. Up to this point, though there may be unimportant diversities in the exposition of words and phrases, there is no material difference of opinion as to the general meaning of the writer: he addressed churches then existing and set before them their sins and duties, and described scenes then present. Here, however, the scene opens into the future, comprehending all the unknown period until Christianity shall finally triumph. The actors are the Son of God, angels, men, Satan, storms, tempests, earthquakes, the pestilence and fire; the scene is heaven, earth, hell. There is no certain designation of places; there is no mention of names, as there is in one prophet of Cyrus and in another of the king of Grecia; there is no designation of time that is necessarily unambiguous; and there are no characteristics of the symbols used that make it antecedently certain that they could be applied only to one class of events. Then, having said so much, make no effort to interpret these seals as referring to persons or historical events in the past, present or future, but simply relate the symbolism to the other symbols in the book. Note that the imagery of the four horses is similar to that in Zechariah, that in the Old Testament the horse is often the emblem of war, and that a classical poet pictures the horses of Rhesus as whiter than snow and swift as the wind; note also that the phrase when the Lamb opened recurs in rhythmical order at the opening of each seal till the last, where a different particle calls particular attention to it. On the summons, observe that the words and see are doubtful, being found in some manuscripts and omitted in others, with the authority about equally divided; under these circumstances we may fairly be guided by the context, and ask to whom the summons is addressed. Not to the seer: he was near already, he had seen the Lamb opening the seal, and there was no object in his drawing near. Nor, as one commentator supposes, to Christ, for it is difficult to believe that the living creature would thus cry to the Lamb who was opening the scroll. The simplest way of answering the question is to ask another — who did come in obedience to the voice? There is but one answer, the horseman. The living beings cry Come, and their cry is responded to by the appearance of the several riders. And what is the spiritual meaning? The living beings represent animated nature, that nature and creation of God which groans and travails in pain, waiting for the manifestation of the sons of God. These summon the emblems of war and pestilence to come on the scene, for these things must needs be, and through these lies the way for the final coming of God’s Christ, for whom creation longs. They bid the pains and troubles come, because they recognise them as the precursors of creation’s true King; and thus their voice has in it an undertone which sighs for the advent of the Prince of Peace, who is to come.

Take the white horse and the crowned horseman with a bow to be the first thing done by Christ himself: for after the Lord ascended into heaven and opened all things, he sent the Holy Spirit, whose words the preachers sent forth as arrows reaching to the human heart, that they might overcome unbelief; and the crown on the head is promised to the preachers by the Holy Spirit. The other three horses very plainly signify the wars, famines and pestilences announced by our Lord in the Gospel. Note that one of the four living creatures speaks, because all four are one; and that Come is said to him who is invited to faith, See to him who saw not. Therefore the white horse is the word of preaching with the Holy Spirit sent into the world, for the Lord says that this Gospel shall be preached throughout the whole world for a testimony to all nations, and then shall come the end. Or note that, seeing the seals are first loosed and the book is then opened, he has purposely changed the accustomed order: for in that he suffered and rose again the Lord taught the Church that he was the end of the law, and in that he ascended into heaven, by the mission of the Holy Spirit, he strengthened the Church with the gift of a more hidden mystery. Then set out the scheme of the seven: in the first seal he beholds the glory of the primitive Church, in the following three the threefold war against it, in the fifth the glory of those who triumph in this war, in the sixth the things which are to come in the time of Antichrist, and that with a brief recapitulation of former events, in the seventh the beginning of eternal rest. Say that we also are admonished by the loud voice of the Gospel to behold the glory of the Lord; that the Lord presides over the Church, which is made whiter than snow by grace, and bears the arms of spiritual teaching against the ungodly, receiving as conqueror a crown in the persons of his own; and that the seer is wisely bidden to observe the opposing horsemen, so that as he derives joy from the prosperity of the Church, he may acquire caution also from its adversity, by foreknowledge of it.

Note that one of the seals means the first, as several copies and versions read one of the seven seals, and as appears from the following seals being called second, third and fourth. Say these seals express events to be fulfilled, and therefore cannot respect the steps towards, and the signs of, Jerusalem’s destruction, and that itself, which had been accomplished some years before the vision of the seals — a vision of which would have been needless. They are called seals because they were sealed among God’s treasures, or resolved on and decreed by him, and because they were hidden and unknown until they came to pass; and when they came to pass they were pledges of what God would do in the destruction of Rome Papal, as here in the destruction of Rome Pagan. For these seals, at least the first six of them, concern the pagan empire and the state of the church in it, and are so many gradual steps to the ruin of it.

Observe that Christ, the Lamb, opens the first seal, and now enters upon the great work of opening and accomplishing the purposes of God towards the church and the world; that one of the ministers of the church calls upon the apostle, with a voice like thunder, to come near and observe what appeared. Then take the vision itself. The Lord Jesus appears riding on a white horse: white horses are generally refused in war, because they make the rider a mark for the enemy, but our Lord Redeemer was sure of the victory and a glorious triumph, and he rides on the white horse of a pure but despised gospel, with great swiftness through the world. He had a bow in his hand: the convictions impressed by the word of God are sharp arrows, they reach at a distance, and though the ministers of the word draw the bow at a venture, God can and will direct it to the joints of the harness — this bow, in the hand of Christ, abides in strength, and never returns empty. A crown was given him, importing that all who receive the gospel must receive Christ as a king and be his loyal and obedient subjects; and when Christ was going to war one would think a helmet had been more proper than a crown, but a crown is given him as the earnest and emblem of victory. He went forth conquering and to conquer: as long as the church continues militant Christ will be conquering, and when he has conquered his enemies in one age he meets with new ones in another — men go on opposing, and Christ goes on conquering, and his former victories are pledges of future victories.

Give the chapter its argument: the opening of the first seal and the white horse; of the second and the red horse; of the third and the black horse and the famine; of the fourth and the pale horse; of the fifth and the souls of men under the altar; of the sixth and the earthquake, the darkening of the sun and moon and the falling of the stars; and then the terrible consternation of the kings and great men of the earth. Remark that the opening of the seals is not merely a declaration of what God will do, but the exhibition of a purpose then accomplished, for whenever the seal is opened the sentence appears to be executed; and note the supposition that from this chapter to the eleventh the calamities which should fall on the enemies of Christianity, and particularly the Jews, are pointed out under various images, as well as the preservation of the Christians under those calamities. Take the first living creature to be probably that with the face of a lion; take Come and see as meaning, attend to what is about to be exhibited; and say it is very likely that all was exhibited before his eyes as in a scene, and that he saw every act represented which was to take place, and all the persons and things which were to be the chief actors. Elsewhere say only that the first of the living creatures is the one who looks forward toward the east.

debates: Whether the seals can be referred to particular historical events at all.
Whether the clause and see belongs in the text.
To whom the summons Come is addressed.
Whether the first six seals concern the pagan empire or the Jews.
What the white horse and its rider signify.
outliers: Barnes states that all agreement among interpreters ends at this chapter, and says why.
Robertson responds by refusing to identify the seals with any persons or events whatever.
Ellicott settles the addressee of the summons by asking instead who obeyed it.
Ellicott makes the living creatures animated nature, summoning war and pestilence because they precede the coming of Christ.
Clarke reports the reading that refers the calamities to the Jews; Gill refuses it as chronologically needless.
Bede sets out a scheme for all seven seals, ending in the beginning of eternal rest.
Henry observes that white horses are refused in war because they make the rider a mark.

2.pericope_label: And I saw, and behold a white horse: and he that sat on him had a bow; and a crown was given unto him: and he went forth conquering, and to conquer. And when he had opened the second seal, I heard the second beast say, Come and see. And there went out another horse that was red: and power was given to him that sat thereon to take peace from the earth, and that they should kill one another: and there was given unto him a great sword

schools.summary: Begin with the question nobody else asks: in what mode was this shown? Was it a series of pictures drawn on successive portions of the volume as one seal was broken after another, or was the description written on the volume so that John read it or heard it read, or was the opening of the seal merely the occasion of a scenic representation? Nothing is said by which this can be determined with certainty, but the most probable supposition is that there was a pictorial representation, and for four reasons: it was something in or on the volume, since he was invited to draw nearer; each thing under the first five seals is capable of being painted; the language is not such as would have been employed if he had merely read the description or heard it read; and the alternative is unnatural and forced — what would be the use of a sealed volume in that case, or of the writing within and without, if the breaking of each seal disclosed nothing but a succession of blank portions? Then state the method for reading any of these symbols: form first a clear conception of what the emblem would naturally convey, assuming the symbol is significant and that there was a reason why a horse was used rather than an eagle or a lion, why white here and red, black and pale after, why a bow in this rider’s hand and a crown on his head; each particular enters into the constitution of the symbol, and something in the event must correspond with each. Where the general symbol is the same, as through the first four seals, the same class of objects is referred to, and the diversity is carried by the colour of the horse and the arms and apparel of the rider. On the second living creature, deny that there is any special significance in which creature speaks: there is no reason in the symbol why this one rather than another should be heard at this seal, and all that is designed is that the living creatures, being emblems of the providential government of God, should be shown concerned in the opening of each of these four seals. On the red horse, say that the emblem cannot be mistaken — as the white denoted prosperity and triumph, this denotes carnage and discord, and the explanation is added at once, that they should kill one another. Press the article: the words are to take the peace from the earth, the previously existing peace, not peace in general, so that the state before was tranquil and what follows is civil slaughter. Then, if the history is to be traced at all, look to the accession of Commodus in the year 180, following the peaceful reigns of Hadrian and the Antonines, when the beloved son of Marcus succeeded amidst the acclamations of the senate and armies and saw around him neither competitor to remove nor enemies to punish. On the words themselves, note that and I saw and behold is a combination frequent in this book; that white seems to be the colour of victory, like the white horse of the Persian kings and the horse ridden by the Roman conqueror in his triumph; that the aorist in and that he might conquer points to ultimate victory; that it is tempting to identify this rider with the rider on the white horse later in the book, whose name is the Word of God, but that the two riders have nothing in common beyond the white horse; that the red is flame-coloured or blood-red; and that the sword here is not the knife carried in a sheath at the girdle but the long sword of battle. Of the clause that they should slay one another, say that this is what war does to perfection. Elsewhere take the rider to be victory itself, and say that all are agreed so far, the crown of triumph and the white horse being obviously the emblems of victory; but that the words that he might conquer carry the thought beyond a mere transient conqueror, and that no picture of Roman world-victory would have conveyed the assured happy feeling the vision was plainly designed to give. Read it therefore as the reflex of the hopes of early Christian thought, the symbol of Christian victory: it was thus their hopes saw Christ, who though ascended went forth in spiritual power conquering. They were right in their faith and wrong in their expectation — right in their faith, that he went forth conquering and would conquer; wrong in their expectation, for the visions of war, famine and death must intervene, and it was through these that the conqueror would be proved more than conqueror. It is perhaps significant of that intervening period of trouble that the rider is armed with a bow: the arrows of his judgments would be sharp among those who refused the sword of his word.

Take the white horse for the ministration of the Gospel in the times of the apostles, which were just now finishing, John being the last of them and the one who saw this vision. The horse, being a swift, majestic and warlike creature, fearless of opposition and war, may design the swift progress of the Gospel in the world, the majesty, power and authority with which it came, and the opposition it met with and bore down before it; and the white colour may denote the purity of Gospel truths, the peace it proclaims, the joy it brings, and the triumph that attends it on account of the victories obtained by it. Note that white horses were used in triumphs in token of victory, and that among the Jews a white horse in a dream is a good sign, a vision of white horses being reckoned an apparition of angels — but say plainly that the rider here is not one of those. On the second seal, take the red horse as an emblem either of the suffering state of the church, answerable to the Smyrnaean church as the purity and power of the Gospel in the former seal answered to the Ephesine; or of the contentions and divisions occasioned among men through the Gospel, which though of a peaceable nature yet, through the corruption and depravity of men, brings not peace but a sword; or rather, and best, of the bloody wars within the period signified by this seal, which came as punishments upon the enemies of the Gospel.

Set the next three seals together and say what they are: a sad prospect of great and desolating judgments with which God punishes those who either refuse or abuse the everlasting gospel. Refuse the narrower readings — though some understand them of the persecutions that befell the church of Christ, and others of the destruction of the Jews, they rather seem more generally to represent God’s terrible judgments, by which he avenges the quarrel of his covenant upon those who make light of it. On the second seal, the red horse signifies the desolating judgment of war; its rider had power to take peace from the earth and to set the inhabitants of the earth killing one another. Who that rider is, whether Christ himself as Lord of hosts or the instruments he raises up to conduct the war, is not clear; but three things are certain: that those who will not submit to the bow of the gospel must expect to be cut in sunder by the sword of divine justice; that Jesus Christ rules and commands not only in the kingdom of grace but in the kingdom of providence; and that the sword of war is a dreadful judgment, taking away peace, one of the greatest blessings, and putting men upon killing one another — men who should love one another and help one another are, in a state of war, set upon killing one another.

Read the first seal as the Gospel system, and point out its excellence, swiftness and purity: the rider is Jesus Christ, the bow is the preaching of the Gospel darting conviction into the hearts of sinners, the crown is the emblem of the kingdom which Christ is to establish on earth, and conquering and to conquer means overcoming and confounding the Jews first and then the Gentiles, spreading more and more the doctrine and influence of the cross over the face of the earth. Or else take the whole series historically. The colour and the bow shooting arrows afar off betoken victory, triumph, prosperity, enlargement of empire and dominion over many people; and though another horseman of quite another kind appears on a white horse later in the book, the one under the first seal must be so understood as to bear a proportion to the horsemen of the second, third and fourth. Nerva succeeded the emperor Domitian at the very time when the Revelation was written, in the year 96; he reigned scarce a year alone, named Trajan for his colleague and successor three months before his death, and died in 98. Trajan’s accession seems to be the dawning of the seven seals. The crown, considering his descent, Trajan could have no hope of attaining, but God gave it him by the hand of Nerva, and then the east soon felt his power; and in the year 108 the already victorious Trajan went forth toward the east, to conquer not only Armenia, Assyria and Mesopotamia but the countries beyond the Tigris, carrying the bounds of the Roman empire to a far greater extent than ever. We find no emperor like him for making conquests: he aimed at nothing else, he lived only to conquer. On the second seal, take the red as a colour suitable to bloodshed, and the rider as war — perhaps also as severe persecution and the martyrdom of the saints. Some say the rider is Christ, others Vespasian, others the Roman armies, others Artabanus king of the Parthians. To take peace from the earth is to deprive Judaea of all tranquillity, and that they should kill one another was literally the case with the Jews while besieged by the Romans, the great sword meaning great influence and success producing terrible carnage. Or date it again: Vespasian in the year 75 had dedicated a temple to Peace, but as soon as Trajan ascended the throne peace was taken from the earth. Decebalus, king of Dacia, which lies westward from Patmos, put the Romans to no small trouble; the war lasted five years and consumed abundance of men on both sides, and was only a prelude to much other bloodshed which followed for a long season. Note lastly that the second living creature looked toward the west, for at each seal it was necessary to turn toward that quarter of the world which it more immediately concerned.

debates: Whether the seer saw pictures in the volume, read a written description, or watched a scene.
Who the rider on the white horse is: the gospel, Christ, victory itself, or the emperor Trajan.
Whether the first two seals concern the Jews and Judaea or the empire and the church at large.
Whether the order of the four living creatures signifies anything.
outliers: Wesley identifies the first two seals with Trajan and the Dacian war, dated to the years 98 to 108.
Ellicott reads the white horse as the reflex of early Christian hope, right in its faith and wrong in its expectation.
Clarke confines the taking of peace to the deprivation of Judaea, fulfilled in the Roman siege.
Henry deliberately generalises the seals against both the persecution and the destruction-of-Jerusalem readings.
Barnes denies that the order of the living creatures carries any meaning at all.

5.pericope_label: And when he had opened the third seal, I heard the third beast say, Come and see. And I beheld, and lo a black horse; and he that sat on him had a pair of balances in his hand. And I heard a voice in the midst of the four beasts say, A measure of wheat for a penny, and three measures of barley for a penny; and see thou hurt not the oil and the wine

schools.summary: Read the black the way the red was read, from the emblem outward, but do not let the colour settle the question. Black is in Scripture the image of fear, of famine, of death — our skin was black like an oven, because of the terrible famine; Judah mourneth and is in deep mourning for the land; all faces shall gather blackness — and the Latin poets use it the same way, of fear as black, and of a grove darkening with black dread, and of all things growing dark around the dying. From the colour, then, we should naturally look for some dire calamity, though the nature of the calamity is not designated by the mere use of the word black: famine, pestilence, oppression, heavy taxation, tyranny or invasion might any of them be denoted, and what the calamity is to be must be determined by what follows in the symbol. Next the balances. The word rendered a pair of balances properly means a yoke, serving to couple anything together, as a yoke for cattle, and hence the beam of a balance; the idea is that something is to be weighed, in order to ascertain either its quantity or its value. Scales are the emblem of justice and equity, and if the balances stood alone we should look under this seal to a time of the exact administration of law, as scales are used now for the rigid application of principle in the courts; but they are also sometimes the emblem of exaction and oppression, as where the balance of deceit is in his hands and he loveth to oppress, and when joined with the sale of corn and fruit by weight they become the symbol of scarcity, as bread by weight does in the law and in Ezekiel. So leave the question open between dearth and severe exaction of revenue, and let the proclamation limit and define it, since the reference to the wheat and barley and to the price fixes the symbol upon the necessaries of life, the productions of the land, the actual capital of the country. Note also that the voice comes not from any one of the four living creatures but from among them, that is, from the throne. On which creature speaks, say plainly that it is not apparent why the third should take a particular interest in this seal, nor is it necessary to show why it was so; the general design seems to be only to represent each of the four as interested in the opening of the seals, and the order in which they did this does not seem to be a matter of importance. Elsewhere keep to the words and the pictures they make: lust of conquest brings bloodshed, but also famine and hunger; black is the colour of mourning and famine; the yoke is the word used of the yoke of slavery and of teaching, and here of a pair of scales evenly balancing; the rider of this black horse, like the spectral figure of hunger, carries in his hand a pair of scales, and this is also one of the fruits of war. Say that the vague as it were a voice, giving a certain mysteriousness to a phrase, is one of the characteristics of this writer’s style, and that the voice is the protest of nature against the horrors of famine. Price it exactly: the measure is less than a quart, enough wheat to keep a man of moderate appetite alive for a day; the penny is the genitive of price, the wages of a day labourer; barley was the food of the poor, cheaper even in famine, and it took more of it to support life, the proportion here being three to one. Then read the last clause as a limit and not a threat: the proclamation forbids famine prices for food, solid and liquid, and the prohibition is addressed to the nameless rider who represents Dearth. Wheat and barley, oil and the vine were the staple foods of Palestine and Asia Minor.

Say who is speaking, and say it against the historical reading. The voice heard in the midst of the four living creatures is not the voice of Agabus to the Apostle Paul — that is, it is not the famine under Claudius which the historical expositors offer as the fulfilment — but rather the voice of Christ, who was in the midst of them. Note that the Ethiopic version adds, as the voice of an eagle. For the rest, mark only that the third seal is opened by the Lamb, as before, and that what is disclosed belongs to the same sealed book.

Take the black horse for the emblem of famine, and say which famine: some think that which took place under Claudius, foretold by Agabus and referred to by our Lord among the signs. The third living creature is the one which had the face of a man. The pair of balances shows that the scarcity would be such that every person must be put under an allowance. Work the arithmetic: the measure here mentioned was a measure of dry things, and though its capacity is not exactly known it is generally agreed to have held as much as one man could consume in a day, while the penny, the Roman denarius, was the ordinary pay of a labourer. So it appears that in this scarcity each might be able to obtain a bare subsistence by his daily labour, but a man could not in such a case provide for a family. Three measures of barley seems to have been the proportion of value between the wheat and the barley, barley being allowed to afford a poor aliment and given to Roman soldiers instead of wheat by way of punishment. Hurt not the oil and the wine means be sparing of these: use them not as delicacies but for necessity, because neither the vines nor the olives will be productive. Or take the whole again as history and doctrine together. Call it black famine, as the ancient poets term it, a fit emblem of mourning and distress. When there is great plenty men scarce think it worth their while to weigh and measure everything, but when there is scarcity they are obliged to deliver out by measure and weight; accordingly these scales signify scarcity. They serve also for a token that all the fruits of the earth, and consequently the whole heavens with their courses and influences, and all the seasons of the year with whatsoever they produce in nature or in states, are subject to Christ; and accordingly his hand is wonderful, not only in wars and victories, but likewise in the whole course of nature. On the price, say the measure was a Grecian measure nearly equal to our quart and was the daily allowance of a slave, and the Roman penny about sevenpence halfpenny English, so that wheat would be near twenty shillings the bushel; and note that this must have been fulfilled while the Grecian measure and the Roman money were still in use, and where that measure was the common measure and this money the current coin. It was so in Egypt under Trajan. Hurt not the oil and the wine means, let there not be a scarcity of everything, let there be some provision left to supply the want of the rest. This also was fulfilled in the reign of Trajan, especially in Egypt, which lay southward from Patmos: in that country, which used to be the granary of the empire, there was an uncommon dearth at the very beginning of his reign, so that he was obliged to supply Egypt itself with corn from other countries, and the same scarcity returned in the thirteenth year of his reign, the harvest failing for want of the rising of the Nile, and that not only in Egypt but in all those other parts of Africa where the Nile uses to overflow. The third living creature looked toward the south.

debates: Whether the black horse means famine only, or oppression and heavy taxation as well.
Whose voice speaks from the midst of the four living creatures.
Whether the famine is the one under Claudius, the one under Trajan, or none in particular.
Whether hurt not the oil and the wine is a limit on the judgment or part of it.
outliers: Gill denies that the voice is Agabus and makes it the voice of Christ, and reports the Ethiopic addition, as the voice of an eagle.
Barnes declines to say why the third living creature speaks at the third seal, holding the order unimportant.
Wesley assigns the third living creature to the south and dates the famine to the dearths in Egypt under Trajan.
Robertson reads the proclamation as a ceiling forbidding famine prices rather than as the famine itself.

7.pericope_label: And when he had opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth beast say, Come and see. And I looked, and behold a pale horse: and his name that sat on him was Death, and Hell followed with him. And power was given unto them over the fourth part of the earth, to kill with sword, and with hunger, and with death, and with the beasts of the earth

schools.summary: Begin with the colour, since the whole peculiarity of this emblem lies in the colour, the rider and the power given him, and in these there is entire harmony. The word properly means pale-green or yellowish-green, like the first shoots of grass, and then pale or yellowish; and it is the appropriate colour to denote the reign of Death, since paleness is one of the most striking effects of death, from whatever cause. Standing alone it would lead us to look for a state of things in which death prevailed in a remarkable manner; and note the gradation, that red would more naturally denote the ravages of death in war, black the ravages of sudden calamity, and the pale would more obviously suggest famine or wasting disease. Then notice what is absent. No description is given of the rider’s aspect, nor does he appear with any emblem — no sword, spear or bow. There is evident scope for the fancy to picture to itself the form of the Destroyer, and just that kind of obscurity about it which contributes to sublimity; and this is why the opening of this seal has furnished occasion for some of the greatest triumphs of the pencil. On the companion, insist on the sense of the word: it denotes the abode of the dead, considered as a place where they dwell, and not in the more restricted sense in which the word is now commonly used, as a place of punishment. The idea is that the dead would be so numerous at the going forth of this horseman that it would seem as if the pale nations of the dead had come again upon the earth. On the commission, take the earth as the Roman world, and do not insist on precisely a fourth part; look rather for some far-spread calamity, some severe visitation which would sweep off great multitudes. Then divide the instruments, for each must mean something the others do not: to kill with sword is war and discord; with hunger is famine, one of the accompaniments of war, where armies ravage a nation, trample down the standing grain, consume the stores, cut off the men who would till the ground, and shut the people up in besieged cities to perish; and with death must then refer to death in some other form, death that seemed to reign without any such visible cause — that is, the pestilence, which is bred by the unburied bodies of the slain, the filth of a camp, the want of food and the crowding together of multitudes in a besieged city. Confirm it from the versions: the Hebrew word for pestilence, which occurs about fifty times in the Old Testament, is rendered by this same Greek word for death. Elsewhere work the words themselves. The adjective is contracted from the word for tender green grass, used of green grass elsewhere in this book, here for yellowish, greenish-yellow — we speak of a sorrel horse, never of a green horse; Zechariah uses a different word, grizzled or variegated; and Homer used this one of the ashen colour of a face blanched by fear, so the pale horse is a symbol of death and of terror. Note the anacoluthon by which the name is attached to the rider, that Death is here personified, and that with him is his inseparable comrade, Hades — the unseen, from the alpha privative and the verb to see — the abode of the dead, the keys of which Christ holds. The verb is imperfect: Hades kept step with Death, whether on the same horse or on another horse by his side or on foot John does not say. Observe that wider authority is given to this rider than to the others, though what part of the earth is included in the fourth part is not indicated; that the four scourges of Ezekiel are here reproduced, with the instrumental case for the inanimate things and a different preposition for the beasts; and that death here seems to mean pestilence, as the Hebrew does — compare the black death for a plague. On the summons at this seal as at the others, say there does not appear to have been any particular reason why the fourth of the living creatures should have made this proclamation rather than either of the others: it was poetic and appropriate to represent each one in his turn as making proclamation.

Change the application here, and say why. The pale horse may be an emblem of the state of the church — pale, though not with persecution, as some think, for through that it was red, but with the hypocrisy and superstition of many of its members, who were paving the way for the man of sin, and on whose account the church was grown sickly and dying. But rather this is an emblem of the sickly and dying state of the Pagan Roman empire, through a complication of judgments upon it hereafter mentioned — war, famine, pestilence and wild beasts. Note only that it is the Lamb who opens this fourth seal of the sealed book, as he opened the others.

Take the pale horse for the symbol of death: pale death was a very usual poetic epithet, and of this symbol there can be no doubt, because it is immediately said that his name that sat on him was Death. Hell following is the grave, or state of the dead, receiving the slain — a very elegant personification. Over the fourth part of the earth means that one fourth of mankind was to feel the desolating effects of this seal. Then distribute the four: to kill with sword is war; with hunger, famine; with death, pestilence; and with the beasts of the earth, lions, tigers, hyenas and the like, which would multiply in consequence of the devastations occasioned by war, famine and pestilence. Or take it structurally and historically together. The pale is suitable to pale death, his rider; and Hades, the representative of the state of separate souls, follows even with him. The four first seals concern living men, and death is therefore properly introduced, Hades being only occasionally mentioned as a companion of death; so the fourth seal reaches to the borders of things invisible, which are comprised in the three last seals. Mark the escalation: what came single and in a lower degree before comes now together, and much more severely. The first seal brought victory with it; in the second was a great sword, but here a scimitar; in the third was moderate dearth, here famine and plague and wild beasts beside. It may well be that from the time of Trajan downwards the fourth part of men upon the earth, that is, within the Roman empire, died by sword, famine, pestilence and wild beasts. At that time, says Aurelius Victor, the Tiber overflowed much more fatally than under Nerva, with a great destruction of houses, and there was a dreadful earthquake through many provinces, and a terrible plague and famine, and many places consumed by fire. Wild beasts have at several times destroyed abundance of men, and undoubtedly there was given them at this time an uncommon fierceness and strength. Then give the mechanism, for it is observable that war brings on scarcity, and scarcity pestilence, through want of wholesome sustenance; and pestilence, by depopulating the country, leaves the few survivors an easier prey to the wild beasts; and thus these judgments make way for one another in the order wherein they are here represented. Conclude that the four horsemen, with their first entrance in the reign of Trajan and with all their entrances in succeeding ages, and with them the whole course of the world and of visible nature, are in all ages subject to Christ, subsisting by his power and serving his will, against the wicked and in defence of the righteous; that herewith a way is paved for the trumpets, which regularly succeed each other; and that the whole prophecy, as to what is future, is confirmed by the clear accomplishment of this part of it. The fourth living creature looked toward the north.

debates: What the pale colour denotes, and whether it points to famine and disease rather than war.
Whether Hades is the abode of the dead or a place of punishment.
Whether the fourth part of the earth is an exact fraction and what earth is meant.
Whether the pale horse applies to the church or to the pagan empire.
outliers: Gill sets aside his own reading of the pale as the church and applies this seal to the empire instead.
Wesley makes the fourth seal the point at which the vision reaches the borders of things invisible.
Wesley supplies a causal chain by which war, famine, pestilence and wild beasts produce one another in order.
Barnes observes that this seal, alone of the four, gives the rider no emblem, and credits the obscurity with its sublimity.

9.pericope_label: And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held

schools.summary: Account first for the change in the staging. The four living creatures are no longer heard as at the opening of the first four seals, and no reason is given for the change; none can be assigned, unless that having represented each of the four in their turn as calling attention to what was about to happen, there seemed to be no necessity or propriety in introducing them again. Say what the seal is: this one pertains to martyrs, as the former did successively to prosperity and triumph, to discord and bloodshed, to oppressive taxation, and to war, famine and pestilence; in a series of woes it was natural and proper that there should be a vision of martyrs. Four points then require elucidation — their position under the altar, their invocation, the robes given them, and the command to wait. On the position: there were two altars in the temple at Jerusalem, and the one here referred to is probably the altar of burnt sacrifice, which stood in front of the temple. Remember, however, that temple and altar were both destroyed before this book was written, so that this is to be regarded merely as a vision. Why they are seen there is not so apparent, but two suggestions explain it: the altar was the place where sin was expiated, and it was natural to represent these redeemed martyrs as seeking refuge there; and it was usual to offer prayer at the altar in connection with the sacrifice for sin, and on the ground of it. The language is such as a Hebrew would naturally use, but the scene should be regarded as undoubtedly laid in heaven, the temple where God resides; the whole representation is that of fleeing to the atonement and pleading with God in connection with the sacrifice for sin. On the word souls, say that this is one of the incidental proofs in the Bible that the soul does not cease to exist at death, and also that it does not cease to be conscious, or sleep till the resurrection: these souls are represented as still in existence, as remembering what had occurred on the earth, as interested in what was taking place, as engaged in prayer. On the invocation, guard it carefully. They did not doubt that God would avenge them; they inquire only how long the vengeance would be delayed, and they appeal to him as holy and true — as one who cannot look with approval on sin, and who is faithful to his people. They do not speak as if actuated by a spirit of revenge, but as if it were proper that there should be an expression of the divine sense of the wrongs done them; it is not right to desire vengeance or revenge, it is right to desire that justice should be done and that the government of God should be vindicated. Note that the word judge may mean either judge us, in the sense of vindicate us, or judge them, that is, our persecutors. Elsewhere fix the altar by the ritual: under, because the blood of the sacrifices was poured at the bottom of the altar, and it is the altar of sacrifice and not of incense, the imagery being drawn from the tabernacle, this altar in heaven being the antitype of that one. Take the souls as the lives, for the life is in the blood, and these lives were given for Christ. Say who the slain are: Christians were slain during the Neronian persecution and now again under Domitian, and a long line of martyrs has followed. The word of God here means, as at the beginning of the book, the confession of loyalty to Christ as opposed to emperor-worship, and the imperfect tense of held suits the repetition of the witness and the death that followed it. Elsewhere again, make the seal a statement about the church itself: it indicates that the mission of the Christian Church can only be carried out in suffering. An altar is seen, and at its foot the tokens of the martyrs who had laid down their lives upon it; the word souls is the equivalent of lives, and the vision tells that their lives had been sacrificed, as the blood of the victims was in the temple service poured out at the foot of the altar, and as St Paul says he is now ready to be poured out. Refuse the doctrinal use flatly: the word souls has been made a resting-place for an argument respecting the intermediate state, and there is no ground for this; it is quite beside the object of the seal, which simply exhibits the sufferings of Christ’s people as the necessary accompaniment of the progress of the gospel. It was because of the word of God and the testimony that the sacred seer himself suffered, and the words remind us that the same issue which he fought the suffering ones of after ages would be fighting.

Note what is absent and date what is present. There is no living creature speaking here, nor horse and rider presented to view. It was now a very dark time, both with respect to the church of God and the ministry of the word, and with respect to the Roman empire. This seal refers to the times of Diocletian and the persecution under him; and instead of the voice of one of the living creatures, John hears the voice of the martyrs.

Explain first why no one calls the apostle to observe at this seal: probably because the decorum of the vision was to be observed, each of the four living creatures having discharged its duty of monitor before; or because the events here opened lay out of the sight, and beyond the time, of the present ministers of the church; or because this seal does not contain a new prophecy of future events, but rather opens a spring of support and consolation to those who had been and still were under great tribulation for the sake of Christ and the gospel. Then take the sight itself, which is very affecting: he saw the souls of the martyrs, and he saw them under the altar, at the foot of the altar of incense, in the most holy place — that is, he saw them in heaven, at the foot of Christ. Draw four things from that. Persecutors can only kill the body, and after that there is no more that they can do; their souls live. God has provided a good place in the better world for those who are faithful to death and are not allowed a place any longer on earth. Holy martyrs are very near to Christ in heaven, and have the highest place there. And it is not their own death but the sacrifice of Christ that gives them a reception into heaven and a reward there: they do not wash their robes in their own blood, but in the blood of the Lamb. Name the cause they suffered in — the word of God and the testimony which they held, for believing the word of God and confessing the truth of it, a profession they held fast without wavering even though they died for it; a noble cause, the best that any man can lay down his life for. On the cry, be exact about the ethics. Even the spirits of just men made perfect retain a proper resentment of the wrong they have sustained by their cruel enemies; and though they die in charity, praying as Christ did that God would forgive them, yet they are desirous that, for the honour of God and of Christ and of the gospel, and for the terror and conviction of others, God will take a just revenge upon the sin of persecution, even while he pardons and saves the persecutors. They commit their cause to him to whom vengeance belongeth and leave it in his hand; they are not for avenging themselves, but leave all to God. And there will be joy in heaven at the destruction of the implacable enemies of Christ and Christianity, as well as at the conversion of other sinners.

Say plainly that no animal and no other being introduces this seal, and that no new event appears to be predicted: the whole is intended to comfort the followers of God under their persecutions, and to encourage them to bear up under their distresses. A symbolical vision was exhibited in which he saw an altar, and under it the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God, martyred for their attachment to Christianity, represented as newly slain victims to idolatry and superstition. And say where that altar stands: the altar is upon earth, not in heaven. Or take the seal structurally. As the four former seals, so the three latter have a close connection with each other, and these all refer to the invisible world: the fifth to the happy dead, particularly the martyrs; the sixth to the unhappy; the seventh to the angels, especially those to whom the trumpets are given. This book describes not only the church warring under Christ and the world warring under Satan, but also the invisible hosts both of heaven and hell, and not only their actions upon earth but their respective removals from earth into a more happy or more miserable state, with the gradual increase of expectation and triumph in heaven and of terror and misery in hell. Under the altar means at the foot of it. Two altars are mentioned in the Revelation, the golden altar of incense and the altar of burnt-offerings, which is the one meant here; at this the souls of the martyrs now prostrate themselves. By and by their blood shall be avenged upon Babylon, but not yet — whence it appears that the plagues in the fourth seal do not concern Rome in particular.

debates: Why no living creature summons the seer at the fifth seal.
Whether the altar is on earth or in heaven, and whether it is the altar of incense or of sacrifice.
Whether the word souls proves anything about the intermediate state.
Whether the martyrs of this seal are those of Nero and Domitian or those of Diocletian.
How the cry for vengeance is to be reconciled with dying in charity.
outliers: Clarke places the altar upon earth and not in heaven, against every other voice here.
Henry alone puts the martyrs at the foot of the altar of incense rather than the altar of sacrifice.
Ellicott denies that the word souls bears on the intermediate state at all, against Barnes who builds on it.
Wesley infers from the delay of vengeance that the plagues of the fourth seal do not concern Rome in particular.

10.pericope_label: And they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth? And white robes were given unto every one of them; and it was said unto them, that they should rest yet for a little season, until their fellowservants also and their brethren, that should be killed as they were, should be fulfilled

schools.summary: Take the cry as a figure and say whose it is. By a dramatic figure the persecuted and slain ones are represented as crying for retribution on their oppressors; but it is not the Christians themselves who cry for vengeance — they prayed as their Lord and as Stephen prayed — any more than it was Abel himself who cried from the ground to God. It was the blood of Abel; the earth disclosed her blood and refused to cover her slain. The forgotten or ignored wrongs of generations come forth from oblivion and cry for vengeance. It is a poetical description, but it is not fiction: the righteous blood shed does fall upon the world in retribution, and the laws of God avenge themselves, though the victims do not live to behold the reward of the ungodly. On the robe, say the victims are not forgotten — there was given to each a white robe, the glistening apparel of the saints; robes of righteousness, and robes of honour, for those who wear them are like God, seeing him as he is and reflecting his image, and are acknowledged to be his as they have acknowledged him to be their God. Persecuted on earth, they are honoured in heaven. Add the sense in which a white robe is given them in the eyes of men: those whose names have been cast out as evil have been honoured by a repentant posterity with the robe of tardy praise, and the excommunicated in one age are often the canonised of the next, for the dull world learns slowly and its purest honours are posthumous. On the rest, guard it: it does not mean that they are to cease their cry for vengeance, for the saints have never cried for this, but that they rest, as the souls of the faithful after they are delivered from the burden of the flesh, in joy and felicity — a rest that is yet a waiting for a little while, till fellow-servants and fellow-sufferers have achieved their work also, since to every disciple a work is given in service and suffering, and till these have borne their witness and fulfilled their course the departed must wait for their perfect consummation and bliss both in body and soul. Elsewhere keep to the grammar. How long is literally until when. The word rendered Lord is the correlative of servant, a nominative articular form used as a vocative, and here alone in this book is it applied to God, though it is applied to Christ elsewhere in the New Testament. The idiom for avenging our blood from those that dwell upon the earth recurs later in this book and in the parable of the unjust judge, a passage which goes far to answer many questions in theodicy. The robe is a flowing robe, an equipment in clothes; the clause that they should rest is sub-final with the future indicative; yet for a little time is the accusative of extension of time, and the rest is perhaps rest from their cry for vengeance and also rest in peace. Until should be fulfilled is a future indefinite temporal clause meaning until the number of them be filled full, a regular Greek idiom; and the participle rendered which should be killed is the regular construction for what is about to be, so that more persecution is foreseen as coming. Where nothing else is offered on these verses, let the margin carry the weight: send the reader to Zechariah’s own how long, to the song of Moses, to the rewarding of the servants at the seventh trumpet, to the white robes and the great tribulation, to the blessed dead who rest from their labours, and to the word that they without us should not be made perfect.

Read the loudness of the cry as evidence. They cried with great ardour and fervency, being very pressing and importunate; and this shows that they were awake, and not asleep — that the soul does not sleep with the body in the grave, nor is it after the death of the body in a state of insensibility and inactivity, as some imagine. Read the robe the same way. Note that some copies and the Syriac read a white robe in the singular. It is a token of their innocence, that they did not suffer or were not slain for any capital crime or immorality they were guilty of; and of the purity and perfection they now enjoy; and of that spiritual delight and pleasure, unspeakable and full of glory, which they now have in the presence of God and Christ; and in short, of that happiness and glory which souls in a separate state, before the resurrection morn, are partakers of, who besides the righteousness of Christ, comparable to fine linen clean and white, walk with Christ in white, in the shining robes of bliss and glory.

Say first that the cry is the blood’s and not the martyrs’. Their blood, like that of Abel, cried for vengeance; we are not to suppose that there was anything like a vindictive spirit in those happy and holy souls who had shed their blood for the testimony of Jesus. We sometimes say blood cries for blood; that is, in the order of divine justice every murderer and every murdering persecutor shall be punished. Then expand the address: sovereign Lord, supreme Ruler, one having and exercising unlimited and uncontrolled authority; holy, in thy own nature, hating iniquity; and true, in all thy promises and threatenings; dost thou not judge the persecutors, and avenge our blood, that is, inflict signal punishment. Take those that dwell on the earth to mean probably the persecuting Jews, for they dwelt upon that land, a form of speech by which Judea is often signified in the New Testament. Take the white robes as emblems of purity, innocence and triumph; and take the little season as a declaration that when the cup of the iniquity of the Jews should be full they should then be punished in a mass — they were determined to proceed farther, and God permits them so to do, reserving the fullness of their punishment till they had filled up the measure of their iniquity. If this book was written before the destruction of Jerusalem, as is most likely, then that destruction is what was to fall upon the Jews, and the little season is what elapsed between their martyrdom, or the date of this book, and the final destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans under Vespasian and Titus about the year 70; and what follows may refer to the destruction of the heathen Roman empire. Or take the cry and the season quite otherwise. This cry did not begin now, but under the first Roman persecution; and the Romans themselves had already avenged the martyrs slain by the Jews upon that whole nation. The martyrs knew their blood would be avenged, but not immediately, as is now shown them. The Greek word for Lord properly signifies the master of a family, and is therefore beautifully used by these, who are peculiarly of the household of God. Both the holiness and truth of God require him to execute judgment and vengeance; there is no impure affection in heaven, and therefore this desire of theirs is pure and suitable to the will of God, the martyrs being concerned for the praise of their Master, of his holiness and truth — and that praise is given him later, where their prayer is changed into a thanksgiving. On the season, say they were told how long and were not left in uncertainty. Two classes of martyrs are specified here, the former killed under heathen Rome, the latter under papal Rome; the former are commanded to rest till the latter are added to them. There were many of the former in the days of John, and the first fruits of the latter died in the thirteenth century. Now a time in this book is 1111 years: this one began in the year 98 and continued to 1209, from Trajan’s persecution to the first crusade against the Waldenses. And mark what is not said: it is not said that immediately after this time is expired vengeance shall be executed, but only that immediately after this time their brethren and fellowservants will come to them. This event will precede the other, and there will be some space between.

debates: Whether it is the martyrs who cry for vengeance or their blood that cries.
Whether the loudness of the cry proves the soul conscious between death and resurrection.
Who is meant by them that dwell on the earth.
How long the little season is, and what event ends it.
Whether resting means ceasing from the cry.
outliers: Gill uses the cry as a proof text against the sleep of the soul, the inference Ellicott refused at the previous verse.
Clarke confines the vengeance to the Jews and ends the little season at the fall of Jerusalem in the year 70.
Wesley measures the season as a chronos of 1111 years running from 98 to 1209.
Ellicott finds a second white robe in the tardy praise of a repentant posterity.
Barnes's notes on both verses survive only as marginal cross-references.

12.pericope_label: And I beheld when he had opened the sixth seal, and, lo, there was a great earthquake; and the sun became black as sackcloth of hair, and the moon became as blood; and the stars of heaven fell unto the earth, even as a fig tree casteth her untimely figs, when she is shaken of a mighty wind. And the heaven departed as a scroll when it is rolled together; and every mountain and island were moved out of their places

schools.summary: Explain the symbols before applying any of them. All the symbols represented in the opening of this seal denote consternation, commotion, changes; but they are all significant, and we are to suppose that something would occur corresponding with each one. It cannot be supposed that these things were represented on the roll in any other way than as pictures, the whole being a species of panoramic representation made to pass before the eyes; and so understood, each could be painted — the heaving ground, the agitated forests, the trembling hills, the falling cities and houses, the sun blackened, the moon turned to blood. On the earthquake: the word denotes a shaking of the earth, whose effect when violent is to open chasms, throw down houses and temples, sink hills and elevate plains, dry up lakes or form them, rend rocks. But since all that occurs in the other seals is symbolical, this is too, and we are not to look for a literal earthquake but for such agitations and changes in the world as would properly be symbolized by one. There are but three literal earthquakes referred to in Scripture — the one before Elijah, the one in Uzziah’s time, and the one at the Saviour’s death; all the rest are emblematical, referring mostly to civil commotions and changes, as when the Lord says he will shake the heavens and the earth and all nations, and as when Isaiah says the earth shall reel to and fro like a drunkard and be removed like a cottage. An earthquake, with no other circumstance to limit it, would merely denote great agitation and commotion, as if states and empires were tumbling to ruin. On the sun: sackcloth was a coarse black cloth, commonly made of hair, used for sacks and for mourning garments, and the idea is that the sun put on a dark, dingy, doleful appearance, as if the very sun should put on the robes of mourning; we are by no means to suppose this would literally occur. On the stars: the language comes from the poetic idea that the sky is a solid concave in which the stars are set, so that when any convulsion takes place they are loosened and fall; and since stars in the Scriptures are symbols of princes and rulers, the natural meaning is that there would be commotions which would unsettle princes and bring them down from their thrones. The untimely figs are winter figs, which grow under the leaves, do not ripen at the proper season, hang upon the trees through the winter, and easily fall off in the spring; the point of the comparison is the ease with which the stars would seem to be shaken from their places, and hence the ease with which princes would be dethroned. On the heaven departing: the heavens are described as spread out, and their passing away is represented as a rolling up. This too is a symbol, and indeed it never can literally occur; the plain meaning is that revolutions would occur in the high places of the earth as if the stars should fall and the very heavens were swept away. And on the mountains and islands: this would denote convulsions in the political or moral world as great as would occur in the physical world if the mountains were removed and the islands changed their places — if thrones and dynasties long established were overthrown, and institutions that seemed fixed and permanent abolished, the symbol would be fulfilled. Elsewhere hold the same line by another route. The word for earthquake is from the verb to shake, and the reference is not to a local earthquake like those so common in Asia Minor. The sackcloth is a coarse garment of hair clinging to one like a sack, worn by mourners, suppliants and prophets leading austere lives, and here the hair is that of the black goat. Apocalyptic pictures all have celestial phenomena following earthquakes. Note that the heaven was parted, and the participle for rolled up gives a vivid picture of the expanse of the sky rolled away as a papyrus roll. Above all, note the precedent: Peter interpreted Joel’s language about the sun turned into darkness and the moon into blood as pointing to the events of the day of Pentecost, and Peter’s interpretation of Joel should make us cautious about too literal an exegesis of these grand symbols.

Clear away the wrong applications first. Interpreters much differ about this seal. Some refer it to the destruction of Jerusalem, because of the likeness of the expressions used here and there; but this was past many years before this seal was opened, and besides, though that time was a day of wrath to the uttermost upon the Jewish people, and it was the Lamb’s day of wrath, taking vengeance on them for their unbelief and rejection of him as the Messiah, yet they had no sense of the Lamb, nor any apprehension of his wrath at that time, nor have they now, but imputed their calamity to their divisions and quarrels among themselves. Others think this seal belongs to the destruction of the Roman empire by the Goths, Huns and Vandals; but it should be observed that the empire stood some hundreds of years after the end of the fifth seal and the opening of this. Then apply it to Constantine, and read the symbols accordingly. The stars of heaven falling are all the inferior deities losing their esteem, worship and honour; for the idol temples being now opened, the idols and statues were exposed to the common people and were found to be stuffed with hay and straw, which brought them into great contempt. And since stars sometimes signify the ministers of the Gospel in the Christian church, and sometimes the priests in the Jewish church, they may here include the idolatrous priests among the heathens, who were discharged by Constantine and had their posts and profits taken away; and Maximinus, a heathen emperor, being beaten by Licinius, killed many of the priests and prophets of his gods, formerly had in great admiration by him, as deceivers and betrayers by whose oracles he was animated to the war, and Licinius in like manner put to death the priests of the new idol at Antioch. On the heaven departing as a scroll, recall that the manner of writing formerly was on rolls of parchment, whence a book is called a volume, and when rolled up the writing within could not be seen, not a syllable nor letter of it. In like manner the Roman empire as Pagan, which was like a large sheet, or rather like the expanse of the heaven stretched out over all the earth, was now, as to the Paganism of it, rolled up together, so that there were no more heathen gods nor heathen priests, no more idolatry to be seen, and not so much as the names of heathen gods to be heard of in the empire.

Say what the shaking is. When the sixth seal was opened there was a great earthquake: the foundations of churches and states would be terribly shaken. Such bold figurative descriptions of great changes abound in the prophecies of Scripture, for these events are emblems, and declare the end of the world and the day of judgment. Dread and terror would seize on all sorts of men, and neither grandeur, riches, valour nor strength can support men at that time. It seems that the overthrow of the paganism of the Roman empire is here meant, the idolaters being described as hiding themselves in their dens and secret caves and vainly seeking to escape ruin. Draw the application: in such a day, when the signs of the times show those who believe God’s word that the King of kings is approaching, Christians are called to a decided course and to a bold confession of Christ and his truth before their fellow men; and whatever they may have to endure, the short contempt of man is to be borne, rather than that shame which is everlasting.

Read the seal as the overthrow of paganism, and identify every symbol. This seal also is opened and introduced by Jesus Christ alone. The great earthquake is a most stupendous change in the civil and religious constitution of the world; and if it refers to Constantine the Great, the change made by his conversion to Christianity might very properly be represented under the emblem of an earthquake. The sun, the ancient pagan government of the Roman empire, was totally darkened, and like a black hair sackcloth was degraded and humbled to the dust. The moon, the ecclesiastical state of the same empire, became as blood: it was totally ruined, its sacred rites abrogated, its priests and religious institutions desecrated, its altars cast down, its temples destroyed or turned into places for Christian worship. The stars of heaven are the gods and goddesses, demi-gods and deified heroes of their poetical and mythological heaven, prostrated indiscriminately, and lying as useless as the figs of a tree shaken down before ripe by a tempestuous wind. The heaven departing as a scroll is the whole system of pagan and idolatrous worship, with all its spiritual, secular and superstitious influence, blasted, shrivelled up and rendered null and void, as a parchment scroll exposed to the action of a strong fire. Every mountain is all the props, supports and dependencies of the empire, whether regal allies, tributary kings, dependent colonies or mercenary troops, moved out of their places so as to stand no longer in the same relation to that empire; and the islands may be the heathen temples, with their precincts and enclosures, cut off from the common people and into which none could come but the privileged. Or read it quite otherwise, and outside history altogether. This sixth seal seems particularly to point out God’s judgment on the wicked departed: the seer saw how the end of the world was even then set before those unhappy spirits, and this representation might be made to them without anything of it being perceived upon earth. The great earthquake is a shaking, not of the earth only but of the heavens, and is a further description of that representation. Take the astronomy as it stands: the stars fell to, or towards, the earth — yea, and so they surely will, let astronomers fix their magnitude as they please. On the figs, say how sublimely the violence of that shaking is expressed by the comparison. And on the scroll, note the rule: when the scripture compares some very great thing with a little thing, the majesty and omnipotence of God, before whom great things are little, is highly exalted. What a mountain is to the land, that an island is to the sea.

debates: Whether the sixth seal means the fall of Jerusalem, the fall of pagan Rome, or the end of the world.
Whether the earthquake, sun, moon and stars are to be taken as figures or as events.
What the falling stars stand for.
Whether the seal is shown to men on earth at all.
outliers: Wesley makes the seal a representation shown to the wicked departed, perceived by no one on earth.
Wesley takes the falling of the stars literally, against every other voice here.
Robertson cites Peter on Joel as a standing warning against literal exegesis of these symbols.
Gill rejects both the Jerusalem and the barbarian-invasion readings before offering his own.

15.pericope_label: And the kings of the earth, and the great men, and the rich men, and the chief captains, and the mighty men, and every bondman, and every free man, hid themselves in the dens and in the rocks of the mountains; and said to the mountains and rocks, Fall on us, and hide us from the face of him that sitteth on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb: for the great day of his wrath is come; and who shall be able to stand?

schools.summary: Say what the whole passage is for: the varied language is evidently meant to denote universal consternation and alarm, as if the earth should be convulsed and the stars fall and the heavens pass away, and this consternation would extend to all classes of men. Then take the ranks one by one. The kings of the earth are all who occupied thrones; the great men are high officers of state; the rich men are named because their wealth would not secure them from destruction; the chief captains are the commanders of armies, who tremble like other men when God appears in judgment; the mighty men are men of great prowess in battle, who now feel they have no power to withstand God. On bondman, be exact: the word does not necessarily denote a slave, though here the connexion seems to demand it, since it stands in contrast with freeman, and there were in fact slaves in the Roman empire; but since this does not refer to the end of the world or the day of judgment, the word determines nothing as to the question whether slavery is to continue on the earth. The dens are the caves in the mountains, and the rocks the crags and fastnesses, both resorted to for safety in times of danger. On the cry, note that the language is found substantially in Hosea and is used by the Saviour himself of the consternation at his coming: it is the state of mind of one who apprehends that God is coming forth with the instruments of his vengeance, and who desires rather to be crushed by falling rocks and hills than by the vengeance of his uplifted arm. It is not said that God would come forth in a visible form, only that their consternation would be as great as if he did. On the wrath of the Lamb, meet the difficulty plainly: there seems to be an incongruity between the words wrath and Lamb, but the word Lamb here is so far a proper name as to be used only to designate the Redeemer, and he comes forth to execute wrath not as a Lamb but as the Son of God who bore that name. It would seem from this that they who dreaded these terrors understood their source, saw that these were divine judgments, and apprehended that the end of the world drew near. Elsewhere hold to the words. The princes are the grandees, the persecuting proconsuls; the chief captains are commanders of thousands, the military tribunes; and not merely those in civil and military authority will be terror-stricken, but the self-satisfied and complacent rich, and the strong, who usually scoff at fear — bondman and freeman being the two extremes of society. The hiding is based on Isaiah. The two imperatives Fall and Hide are in the tense of urgency, do it now, and come in inverted order from Hosea, quoted by Jesus on the way to the Cross. What sinners dread most is not death, but the revealed Presence of God. And from the wrath of the Lamb is the repetition of the grave irony of the fifth chapter: the Lamb is the Lion again in the terribleness of his wrath. On the last verse, note that the great day is a phrase of the Old Testament prophets, and that their wrath puts the wrath of God and of the Lamb on an equality. Report the view that this language about the great day having come is the mistaken cry of men in terror caused by the portents bursting upon them, and grant there is something to be said for it, since it denies that John commits himself to the position that this is the end of the ages. The closing question is rhetorical, apparently from the frightened crowds, and the only possible answer to that cry is the command of Jesus to keep awake on every occasion, praying that you may get strength to stand — the very form of the word. Elsewhere again, make it the question of questions. The thought is derived from Malachi: every advent of Christ is the advent of one whose fan is in his hand and who will thoroughly purge his floor, whether the advent in the flesh, or the advents in providence — the fall of Jerusalem, the overthrow of Pagan Rome, the convulsions of the Reformation and Revolution epochs — and much more the closing personal advent. Christ’s own answer is that apart from him we can do nothing, and St Paul’s parallel counsel is to take the whole armour of God, that you may be able to withstand in the evil day and, having done all, to stand. Then say where the answer lies: the sixth seal does not give us a completed picture — the whole world is stirred and startled at the tread of the approaching Christ, and then the vision melts away, and one asks what is left for the seventh seal to tell. The answer is given in the next chapter: they shall stand who are sealed with the seal of the living God; in the midst of the shaking of all things there is a kingdom which cannot be shaken.

Name the ranks and then name the men. The kings of the earth and the great men are the Roman emperors and other principal magistrates, governors of provinces and cities. They said to the mountains and rocks, Fall on us: that is, they chose death rather than life. Diocletian, being invited by Constantine to a marriage feast, excused himself by reason of his old age; but receiving threatening letters in which he was charged with having favoured Maxentius and Maximinus, he poisoned himself, and others of the emperors are said to have laid violent hands upon themselves. On the last verse, note that the Vulgate Latin and Syriac versions read of their wrath — both of him that sits upon the throne and of the Lamb — against the heathen gods and heathen persecutors, in answer to the cry of the martyrs at the fifth seal.

Identify the ranks with the defeated pagan order. The kings of the earth and the rest are all the secular powers who had endeavoured to support the pagan worship by authority, influence, riches, political wisdom and military skill; every bondman means all slaves, who were in life and limb addicted to their masters or owners; and every freeman means those who had been manumitted, commonly called freedmen, attached through gratitude to the families of their liberators. All hid themselves: they were astonished at the total overthrow of the heathen empire and the revolution which had then taken place. The cry to the mountains and rocks denotes the strongest perturbation and alarm; they preferred any kind of death to that which they apprehended from this most awful revolution. They now saw that all these terrible judgments came from the Almighty, and that Christ, the author of Christianity, was judging, condemning and destroying them for their cruel persecutions of his followers. The great day of his wrath is the decisive and manifest time in which he will execute judgment on the oppressors of his people, and no might can prevail against the might of God. Say that all this may literally apply to the final destruction of Jerusalem and to the revolution in the Roman empire under Constantine; some apply it to the day of judgment, but it does not seem to have that awful event in view. Justify the figures by precedent: the fall of Babylon, Idumea, Judah, Egypt and Jerusalem has been described by the prophets in language equally pompous, figurative and strong, and it is certain that the fall of none of these was of greater consequence to the world than the fall of the pagan Roman empire, when the great lights of the heathen world, the powers civil and ecclesiastical, were all eclipsed and obscured, the heathen emperors were slain, the heathen priests and augurs extirpated, the officers and magistrates removed, the temples demolished and their revenues devoted to better uses. Add the rule of style: it is customary with the prophets, after they have described a thing in the most symbolical and figurative manner, to represent the same again in plainer language, and the same method is observed here — the kings of the earth means Maximin, Galerius, Maxentius, Licinius and the rest, with all their adherents and followers, so routed and dispersed that they hid themselves in dens. This is therefore a triumph of Christ over his heathen enemies, and a triumph after a severe persecution; and Galerius, Maximin and Licinius made even a public confession of their guilt, recalled their decrees and edicts against the Christians, and acknowledged the just judgments of God and of Christ in their own destruction. Or read the verses quite plainly. The kings of the earth are they who had been so in their day; the great men and chief captains are the generals and nobles; they hid themselves so far as in them lay. There are rocks on the plains also, but these were rocks on high, which they besought to fall upon them — rocks which were tottering already. And hide us from the face of him: that face which is against the ungodly.

debates: Whether the terror of this passage belongs to the fall of pagan Rome or to the day of judgment.
Whether the declaration that the great day is come is the seer’s or the crowd’s mistaken cry.
How wrath can be predicated of a Lamb.
Who is able to stand, and where the answer is given.
outliers: Barnes pauses on the word bondman to deny that the verse settles anything about slavery.
Gill names Diocletian’s suicide as the fulfilment of the cry to the mountains.
Robertson reports the view that the crowd, not the seer, declares the great day come.
Ellicott answers the closing question from the next chapter, by the sealing of the servants of God.
